prompt: Write a spoken word piece from the perspective of a citizen living under a pandemic quarantine enforcement system. She describes, in precise technical detail, how the system tracks her location in real time, how it identified everyone she contacted, how it geofences her apartment and sends automated alerts when she steps outside the radius, and how all of this — her movements, her contacts, her compliance record — flows into a permanent government database. She wants the audience to understand the engineering. Make the technical architecture vivid inside the emotional experience.
response:
# Forty-Seven Days Inside the Radius

*for the ones who got the ping*

---

They start with the phone.

I need you to understand that. Before the swab, before the diagnosis,
before the woman in the hazmat suit
told me to go home and stay home—
they started with the phone.

Not a call. Not a person. A silent registration.
My positive result hit the national disease reporting API
and triggered an automated case event
in the Epidemic Intelligence Platform—
that's what they actually call it, *intelligence*,
like my fever was a state secret—
and within ninety seconds,
my IMSI number, my International Mobile Subscriber Identity,
the fifteen-digit string that *is* me
to every cell tower I've ever whispered past,
was flagged in the telecom bridge layer
and my carrier began retroactive location polling.

Not GPS. I want you to hear this.
Not the satellite constellation, not yet.
First: **cell tower triangulation.**
My phone pings the nearest tower every seven seconds
just to stay registered on the network.
They don't need an app for this. They don't need my permission.
The carrier already logs it—
tower ID, signal strength, timing advance—
and from three towers they can trilaterate my position
to about a fifty-meter radius in the city,
two hundred in the suburbs,
and that was enough,
that was *more* than enough
to reconstruct fourteen days of everywhere I'd been.

Fourteen days. They call it the **contact trace window.**
I call it the last two weeks of my life
unspooled like thread from a bobbin
and pinned to a map.

---

The health authority analyst—
I know there was one, a person, at least at the start—
pulled my **CDR**, my Call Detail Records,
which is the polite name for the fact
that every call I made, every text I sent,
every silent handoff from tower to tower
as I walked to the pharmacy,
as I rode the bus to my mother's house,
as I sat in the park on the bench by the fountain
and felt fine, *felt completely fine*—
all of it was already archived
in the carrier's lawful intercept infrastructure,
which was built for court orders and counterterrorism
but has a pandemic exception now,
a clean little API endpoint
that the health authority hits
with my IMSI and a date range
and gets back a JSON file
containing every tower my phone touched
with timestamps accurate to the second.

They fed that to the **co-location engine.**

This is the part that makes me lie awake.

The co-location engine takes my tower pings
and cross-references them against
*every other phone* that pinged the same tower
within the same time window.
The threshold is fifteen minutes and fifty meters.
Fifteen minutes. The length of a conversation.
The length of standing in line at the grocery store.
The length of sitting across from my friend David
at the noodle shop on Eleventh Street
while he told me his marriage was falling apart
and I reached across the table and held his hand.

The engine doesn't know about the hand.
It knows that IMSI 460-07-2281-XXXXX
and IMSI 460-07-3349-XXXXX
were served by the same sector antenna
of tower CHN-BJ-40872
from 12:47:22 to 13:24:08
and that this constitutes a **close contact event**
with a confidence score of 0.87.

David got the text eighteen minutes later.

---

Now the geofence.

When I got home—
and I want to say *my* home, I want to claim it,
but it doesn't feel like mine anymore,
it feels like a coordinate—
when I got to **39.9042° N, 116.4074° E**,
which is what I am now, a latitude and a longitude
with a cough,
the system drew a circle.

Two hundred meters. That's the **compliance radius.**
It's not a physical fence. There's no wire.
It's a polygon defined in a geospatial database,
a set of vertices stored in PostGIS or something like it,
and my phone is the ankle bracelet
I carry voluntarily
because if I turn it off
they'll know that too—
the *absence* of a ping is itself a ping,
a null event that triggers an alert
in the monitoring dashboard
that someone, somewhere, is watching,
or more likely no one is watching,
more likely it's a rule engine,
a script that runs every thirty seconds:

```
IF device_last_seen > 10 minutes
OR device_location OUTSIDE geofence_polygon
THEN trigger_alert(case_id, alert_type, timestamp)
```

That's it. That's the whole tyranny.
Twelve lines of code and a cron job.

---

The first time I stepped outside the radius
I didn't even know I'd done it.

I walked to the dumpster at the end of the alley.
The dumpster is two hundred and thirty meters
from the centroid of my apartment.
Thirty meters past the edge of the circle.
I was carrying a trash bag and wearing slippers
and the system saw me cross the boundary
because my phone's GPS chipset—
now they *were* using GPS,
the full constellation, American NAVSTAR and Chinese BeiDou,
dual-frequency, L1 and L5 bands,
accurate to three meters under open sky—
reported my position to the quarantine app
which reported to the cloud endpoint
which wrote a row to the violations table
which triggered the alert
which sent me a push notification
that arrived with a sound like a doorbell,
a gentle, *almost kind* sound,
that said:

**⚠️ You have left your designated quarantine area. Please return immediately. This event has been recorded.**

*This event has been recorded.*

I stood there holding the trash bag
and the phone buzzed in my pocket
like a small animal reminding me
it was alive.

---

I want to tell you about the database.

Not because I understand databases.
Because I need you to understand
that there *is* one,
that everything I'm describing doesn't evaporate,
doesn't dissolve after my fever breaks,
doesn't get erased when they lift the quarantine order.

It's a **permanent record.**

My case ID is linked to my national identity number.
My national identity number is linked to my phone.
My phone is linked to fourteen days of movement history.
My movement history is linked to one hundred and six
other human beings
whose phones were near my phone,
and their names are linked to my name
in a **contact graph**—
a node-and-edge data structure
where I am a node
and David is a node
and the woman I stood behind at the pharmacy
whose name I never knew
is a node,
and the edges between us are weighted
by duration and proximity and probability,
and the whole graph is stored
and queryable
and *will be there next year*
when someone asks the system
a question I can't predict.

The schema has a field called `compliance_score`.
It's a float. A decimal number between zero and one.
Mine is 0.94 because of the dumpster.
I don't know what it will be used for.
I don't know who will query it.
I don't know if it will follow me
to a job application, a ## border crossing, a loan.

I know it exists.
I know it is a column in a table
in a database on a server
in a facility I will never see,
and that it describes me
with the authority of a number,
which is the only authority
that systems understand.

---

On day twenty-three I stood at my window
and watched a drone fly down the street.

Not a metaphor. A quadcopter.
White, about a meter across,
with a downward-facing camera
and a thermal imaging sensor
and a loudspeaker that said, in a recorded voice,
*Please return to your residence.*
It wasn't talking to me. I was in my residence.
It was talking to someone on the sidewalk below
who was standing still, looking up at it,
and I thought:

the camera sees a body,
the thermal sensor confirms the body is warm,
the onboard CV model—convolutional neural network,
probably YOLOv5 or something newer—
draws a bounding box around the body,
the system checks whether the body's location
matches any active geofence,
and if the body is outside its circle,
the loudspeaker speaks.

The person on the sidewalk went inside.
The drone banked left and continued down the block,
scanning, scanning,
and I pressed my hand against the glass
and my phone sat on the table behind me,
quiet for now,
logging my coordinates every thirty seconds
to confirm I was still
where I was supposed to be.

---

I want to be fair.

I want to say: I know why they built it.
I know the virus was killing people.
I know the hospitals were full.
I know that contact tracing saves lives,
that quarantine saves lives,
that the math of exponential spread
is merciless and real
and that somewhere in the architecture
there is a genuine intention
to keep people like my mother alive.

I know this.

And I need you to hold that
in the same hand
as this:

The system does not know
why David was crying at the noodle shop.
The system does not know
that I walked to the dumpster in my slippers
because the trash was attracting rats
and I was scared of the rats
more than I was scared of the fine.
The system does not know
that on day thirty-one I sat on the floor
and stopped eating
and the phone kept pinging my location
every thirty seconds
to confirm I was compliant,
to confirm I was still inside the circle,
and it had no field,
no column,
no data type
for the fact that I was disappearing
in a way no sensor could detect.

---

On day forty-seven they sent me a text.

**Your quarantine period has ended. Thank you for your cooperation. Your compliance record has been updated.**

I opened the door.
I stood in the hallway.
I walked to the elevator and pressed the button
and rode it to the ground floor
and stepped outside
and my phone did not buzz.

No gentle doorbell sound.
No push notification.
No alert.

And I stood there on the sidewalk
in the sunlight
and I waited for something to feel different
but the GPS chipset was still active
and the carrier was still logging
and the app was still installed
and the database still had my name
and my compliance score
and my one hundred and six contacts
and the dumpster
and the thirty meters
and the timestamp of every second
of every day
I was inside.

I am outside now.

I am outside now
and I am still
in the system.

I am outside now
and the system
is still
inside me.

---

*[silence]*

*[she puts the phone down on the stage]*

*[she walks away from it]*

*[it stays lit]*
